summary: The parts of a card are name, mana cost, illustration, color indicator, type line, expansion symbol, text box, power and toughness, loyalty, defense, hand modifier, life modifier, illustration credit, legal text, and collector number.
Some parts of a card are also characteristics of the object that has them.
Some objects that aren’t cards (tokens, copies of cards, and copies of spells) have some of the parts of a card, but only the ones that are also characteristics.
The name of a card is printed on its upper left corner.
A card’s name is always considered to be the English version of its name, regardless of printed language.
Two or more objects have the same name if they have at least one name in common, even if one or more of those objects have additional names.
Some spells and abilities refer to two or more objects with different names.
Some spells or abilities check if one object has a different name than a second object or group of objects.
Some cards with different English names are treated as though they had the same English name.
For the purposes of all rules, abilities, and effects that refer to a card’s name, objects with interchangeable names have the same name.
For the purposes of deck construction and format legality, cards with interchangeable names have the same name.

If a card has later printings with interchangeable names, the later printings will have an interchangeable names indicator in the bottom left-hand corner referring to the original printing’s three-letter set code and collector number (see rule 213.1d).
If an effect instructs a player to choose a card name, the player must choose the name of a card in the Oracle card reference.
If a player is instructed to choose a card name with certain characteristics, the player must choose the name of a card whose Oracle text matches those characteristics.
If a player wants to choose the name of a split card, the player must choose the name of one of its halves, but not both.
If a player wants to choose a flip card’s alternative name, the player may do so.
If a player wants to choose the name of the back face of a double-faced card, the player may do so.
If a player wants to choose the name of the combined back face of a meld pair, the player may do so.
If a player wants to choose an adventurer card’s alternative name, the player may do so.
Some cards have interchangeable names (see rule 201.3).
Text that refers to the object it’s on by name means just that particular object and not any other objects with that name, regardless of any name changes caused by game effects.

If an ability’s effect grants another ability to an object, and that second ability refers to that first ability’s source by name, the name refers only to the specific object which is that first ability’s source.

If an ability of an object refers to that object by name, and an object with a different name gains that ability, each instance of the first name in the gained ability that refers to the first object by name should be treated as the second name.
Text printed on some cards refers to that card by a shortened version of its name.
Promotional or alternate-art versions of some cards feature a secondary title bar below the name line.
A card’s mana cost is indicated by mana symbols near the top of the card.
The mana cost of an object represents what a player must spend from their mana pool to cast that card.
Some objects have no mana cost.
An object is the color or colors of the mana symbols in its mana cost, regardless of the color of its frame.
The five colors are white, blue, black, red, and green.
Objects with no colored mana symbols in their mana costs are colorless.
An object with two or more different colored mana symbols in its mana cost is each of the colors of those mana symbols.
An object with one or more hybrid mana symbols and/or Phyrexian mana symbols in its mana cost is all of the colors of those mana symbols, in addition to any other colors the object might be.
An object may have a color indicator printed to the left of the type line.
Effects may change an object’s color, give a color to a colorless object, or make a colored object become colorless; see rule 105.3.
The mana value of an object is a number equal to the total amount of mana in its mana cost, regardless of color.
The mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0, unless that object is the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell, or it is a melded permanent.
The mana value of the back face of a nonmodal double-faced permanent or spell’s back face is calculated as though it had the mana cost of its front face.
The mana value of a melded permanent is calculated as though it had the combined mana cost of the front faces of each card that represents it.
The mana value of a split card not on the stack or of a fused split spell on the stack is determined from the combined mana costs of its halves.

When calculating the mana value of an object with an {X} in its mana cost, X is treated as 0 while the object is not on the stack, and X is treated as the number chosen for it while the object is on the stack.
When calculating the mana value of an object with a hybrid mana symbol in its mana cost, use the largest component of each hybrid symbol.
Each Phyrexian mana symbol in a card’s mana cost contributes 1 to its mana value.
Any additional cost listed in an object’s rules text or imposed by an effect isn’t part of the mana cost.
The illustration is printed on the upper half of a card and has no effect on game play.
The color indicator is printed to the left of the type line directly below the illustration.
An object with a color indicator is each color denoted by that color indicator.
The type line is printed directly below the illustration.
Some effects set an object’s card type.
Some effects change an object’s card type, supertype, or subtype but specify that the object retains a prior card type, supertype, or subtype.
Card Types
The card types are artifact, battle, conspiracy, creature, dungeon, enchantment, instant, kindred, land, phenomenon, plane, planeswalker, scheme, sorcery, and vanguard.
Some objects have more than one card type (for example, an artifact creature).
Tokens have card types even though they aren’t cards.
Subtypes
A card can have one or more subtypes printed on its type line.
Subtypes of each card type except creature and plane are always single words and are listed after a long dash.
If a card with multiple card types has one or more subtypes, each subtype is correlated to its appropriate card type.
An object can’t gain a subtype that doesn’t correspond to one of that object’s types.
If an effect instructs a player to choose a subtype, that player must choose one, and only one, existing subtype, and the subtype must be for the appropriate card type.
Many cards were printed with subtypes that are now obsolete.
Artifacts have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called artifact types.
Enchantments have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called enchantment types.
Lands have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called land types.
Planeswalkers have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called planeswalker types.
Instants and sorceries share their lists of subtypes; these subtypes are called spell types.
Creatures and kindreds share their lists of subtypes; these subtypes are called creature types.
Planes have their own unique set of subtypes; these subtypes are called planar types.
One dungeon card (Undercity) has a subtype; this subtype is called a dungeon type.
Battles have a unique subtype, called a battle type.
Phenomenon cards, scheme cards, vanguard cards, and conspiracy cards have no subtypes.
Supertypes
An object can have one or more supertypes.
An object’s supertype is independent of its card type and subtype, even though some supertypes are closely identified with specific card types.
Any land with the supertype “basic” is a basic land.
Any permanent with the supertype “legendary” is subject to the state-based action for legendary permanents, also called the “legend rule” (see rule 704.5j).
Any instant or sorcery spell with the supertype “legendary” is subject to a casting restriction.
Any permanent with the supertype “world” is subject to the state-based action for world permanents, also called the “world rule” (see rule 704.5k).
Any permanent with the supertype “snow” is a snow permanent.
Any scheme card with the supertype “ongoing” is exempt from the state-based action for schemes (see rule 704.6e).
The expansion symbol indicates which Magic set a card is from.
The color of the expansion symbol indicates the rarity of the card within its set.
Previously, a spell or ability that affected cards from a particular set checked for that set’s expansion symbol.
One card (City in a Bottle) refers to permanents and cards with a name originally printed in the Arabian Nights™ expansion.
One card (Golgothian Sylex) refers to permanents with a name originally printed in the Antiquities™ expansion.
One card (Apocalypse Chime) refers to permanents with a name originally printed in the Homelands™ expansion.

Players may include cards from any printing in their constructed decks if those cards appear in sets allowed in that format (or those cards are specifically allowed by the Magic: The Gathering Tournament Rules).
The full list of expansions and expansion symbols can be found in the Card Set Archive section of the Magic website (Magic.Wizards.com/en/products/card-set-archive).
The text box is printed on the lower half of the card.
The text box may also contain italicized text that has no game function.
Reminder text is italicized text within parentheses that summarizes a rule that applies to that card.
Flavor text is italicized text that, like the illustration, adds artistic appeal to the game.
An ability word appears in italics at the beginning of some abilities.
Similar to ability words, flavor words appear in italics at the beginning of some abilities.
Some cards have decorative icons in the background of their text boxes.
The chaos symbol appears in the text box of each plane card to the left of a triggered ability that triggers whenever chaos ensues.
One card (Cryptic Spires) has a set of symbols below the text box that represent each color and an ability that instructs a player to circle two of those colors as they create their deck.
A creature card has two numbers separated by a slash printed in its lower right corner.
Rather than a fixed number, some creature cards have power and/or toughness that includes a star (*).
The card may have a characteristic-defining ability that sets its power and/or toughness according to some stated condition.

The card may have a static ability that creates a replacement effect that sets the creature’s power and toughness to one of a number of specific values as it enters the battlefield or is turned face up.
A noncreature permanent has no power or toughness, even if it’s a card with a power and toughness printed on it (such as a Vehicle).

If an effect would be created that sets the base power and/or toughness of a noncreature permanent, or otherwise modifies its power and/or toughness, that effect is created even though it doesn’t do anything unless that permanent becomes a creature.
Some effects refer to a creature’s “base power,” “base toughness,” or “base power and toughness.”
Effects that set a creature’s power and/or toughness to specific values may refer to base power and/or toughness.
Some effects check a creature’s base power and/or toughness.
If a creature somehow has no value for its power, its power is 0.
Each planeswalker card has a loyalty number printed in its lower right corner.
An activated ability with a loyalty symbol in its cost is a loyalty ability.
Each battle card has a defense number printed in its lower right corner.
Each vanguard card has a hand modifier printed in its lower left corner.
Each vanguard card has a life modifier printed in its lower right corner.
Each card features text printed below the text box that has no effect on game play.
Most card sets feature collector numbers.
A card’s rarity is indicated with a single letter following the collector number.
Some promotional cards include information to indicate the specific promotion the card is associated with.
Some cards with interchangeable names include information about a specific version of a card with that interchangeable name.
The three-character code representing the set in which a card is printed and the two-character code representing the language in which a card is printed are separated by a bullet point.
The illustration credit for a card follows the paintbrush icon or, on older cards, the abbreviation “Illus.”
Legal text (the fine print at the bottom or bottom-right of the card) lists the trademark and copyright information.
